blocks.h: Why `k %= n` and why the early return when `k == 0`?
p: Without the modulo, large k would walk around the ring many times. If `k % n == 0` the code would otherwise compute `range(n - 1)`, reach the tail, set `tail.next = None` and reconnect it to head: harmless here, but the early return avoids needless work.

bullets: Time: O(n) — one pass to find the length and tail, one partial pass to the cut point.

61.takeaway: Rotate a list by making it a ring: find the length, reduce k modulo n, cut after the (n−k)-th node.

Border guard without negative indexing (`grid[-1]` would silently wrap!)
Cheaper of the two ways to arrive
DP transition for 'only right or down' moves
Overwrites each cell with its best cumulative sum
In-place DP: the original value is no longer needed once used
The answer once the table is filled

p: `[[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]]`. Each cell becomes its own cost plus the cheaper of the cumulative sums above and to the left. Final grid: [[1, 4, 5], [2, 7, 6], [6, 8, 7]].

In row 0 there is no cell above, and in column 0 no cell to the left. Reading `grid[i-1][j]` with `i = 0` would silently use the last row (Python negative indexing), giving wrong answers rather than an error. `inf` makes the missing side lose every `min`, so row 0 and column 0 only accumulate along the edge.

Because moves are only right or down, any path to a cell must come from directly above or directly left. The best path to a cell is its cost plus the best path to one of those two. Greedy choices at each step would fail; the DP compares complete cumulative costs.

bullets: Space: O(1) extra, since the input grid is overwritten (use a copy if the input must be preserved).

64.takeaway: Grid DP with two incoming directions: dp[i][j] = cost + min(from above, from left), reusing the grid as the table.

p: `'11' + '1'` (3 + 1). Digits are consumed from the right; `res` collects bits least-significant first. Reversed, it reads `100`.

blocks.h: Why does the loop include `or carry`?
p: After both strings are exhausted a carry may still be pending. Here the third iteration has `i = -1`, `j = -1` but `carry = 1`, producing the leading `1`. Without `or carry` the answer would be `'00'`.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Ways to stand on step 0 (`a`) and step 1 (`b`)
Base cases of the recurrence ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2)
n−1 updates move `b` from step 1 up to step n
For n = 1 the loop doesn't run and the answer is 1
Simultaneous assignment: the right side is computed with the old values
Slides the two-value window forward without a temp variable

p: `n = 5` needs 4 updates. `b` is always the number of ways to reach the current step, so the answer is 8:

The last move onto step i was either a 1-step from i−1 or a 2-step from i−2, and the two groups never overlap. So ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2), the Fibonacci recurrence. Storing only the last two values removes the O(n) array.
Writing `a = b; b = a + b` would make the second line use the new `a`, giving `b + b`. The tuple form `a, b = b, a + b` evaluates the right side first, so `a + b` uses the old values.

70.takeaway: 1-D DP compressed to two rolling values: ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2), the Fibonacci pattern.

p: `[[0,1,2,0],[3,4,5,2],[1,3,1,5]]`: rows containing a zero = [0], columns = [0, 3]. Every cell in those rows or columns becomes 0:

If you zeroed as soon as you saw a 0, the new zeros would be mistaken for original zeros, and the whole matrix would turn to 0. Two passes (collect, then write) keep the decision based on the original values only.
